accepted.s:
Under the Government of India Act, 1858, the powers of the Crown in relation to India were exercised through which of the following?
1. Secretary of State for India
2. Council of India
3. Board of Control
4. Court of Directors
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The Government of India Act, 1858 vested the Crown's powers in the Secretary of State for India, assisted by a 15-member Council of India. The Board of Control and Court of Directors were abolished.
accepted.tq: Identify the institutions abolished by the Act before selecting the surviving administrative arrangement.
accepted.sec: Government of India Act 1858 - Secretary of State, Council of India, end of dual control  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The Secretary of State for India created by the Government of India Act, 1858 was a member of the:
accepted.x: The Secretary of State for India was a member of the British Cabinet and exercised the powers of the Crown in relation to India.
accepted.tq: Match the newly created office with its constitutional position rather than with its advisory body.
accepted.sec: Government of India Act 1858 - Secretary of State, Council of India, end of dual control  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Council of India under the Government of India Act, 1858:
1. It consisted of 15 members.
2. It advised the Secretary of State for India.
3. It continued in existence until the Government of India Act, 1935.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The Council of India consisted of 15 members and advised the Secretary of State. It was abolished by the Government of India Act, 1935, making statement 3 false.
accepted.tq: The time-limit statement is tested against the later abolition of the Council.
accepted.sec: Government of India Act 1858 - Secretary of State, Council of India, end of dual control  [APPSC]

accepted.s: The expression ‘double government’ in the administration of British India referred principally to the joint control exercised by the:
o: Board of Control and Court of Directors
accepted.x: The system of double government operated through the Board of Control and the Court of Directors. Both bodies were abolished by the Government of India Act, 1858.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the executive office created in 1858 and the two bodies that were abolished.
accepted.sec: Government of India Act 1858 - Secretary of State, Council of India, end of dual control  [APPSC]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the change in the designation of the Governor-General after the Government of India Act, 1858?
o: The Governor-General became the elected head of the Central Legislative Council.
The Governor-General became the Secretary of State for India.
The Governor-General was replaced by the President of the Council of India.
The Governor-General was also styled the Viceroy as the representative of the Crown.
accepted.x: After 1858, the Governor-General of India was also styled the Viceroy, signifying his role as the representative of the Crown. Lord Canning was the first holder of this position.
accepted.tq: Focus on the precise institutional meaning of the new title rather than on a change of office-holder.
accepted.sec: Government of India Act 1858 - Secretary of State, Council of India, end of dual control  [APPSC]

accepted.s:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
A. Pitt’s India Act
B. Act of 1786
C. Charter Act of 1793
D. Government of India Act, 1858
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The correct order is Pitt’s India Act, 1784; Charter Act of 1793; Act of 1786 is actually earlier than 1793, so the correct chronological sequence is A, B, C, D.
accepted.tq: Place the dated Acts first and check the close pair of 1786 and 1793 carefully.
accepted.sec: Governor-General's power to override his council → Act  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The Act of 1786 is particularly significant because it empowered the Governor-General to:
o: override his Council in special circumstances
accepted.x: The Act of 1786 empowered the Governor-General to override his Council in special circumstances. This provision was initially given to Lord Cornwallis.
accepted.tq: Link the exceptional power with the specific Act instead of with the later Charter Acts.
accepted.sec: Governor-General's power to override his council → Act  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: With reference to the extension of the power granted by the Act of 1786, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Charter Act of 1813 extended it only to provincial Governors.
The Charter Act of 1793 extended it to all future Governors-General and Presidency Governors.
The Indian Councils Act, 1861 extended it to elected members.
The Government of India Act, 1858 extended it to the Secretary of State.
accepted.x: The Charter Act of 1793 extended the overriding power to all future Governors-General and Governors of the Presidencies.
accepted.tq: Use the successive-Act trap by distinguishing the original grant from its later extension.
accepted.sec: Governor-General's power to override his council → Act  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the principal constitutional significance of the Charter Act of 1853?
o: It abolished the office of the Governor-General.
It separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General’s Council.
It transferred all legislative power to provincial councils.
It introduced dyarchy in the provinces.
accepted.x: The Charter Act of 1853 separated the legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General’s Council, marking an important step in the development of legislative institutions.
accepted.tq: Distinguish institutional separation under 1853 from provincial dyarchy under 1919.
accepted.sec: Separation of legislative and executive functions → Act  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following statements regarding Indian participation in the civil services is correct?
o: The Macaulay Committee was established in 1861 to recruit provincial ministers.
The Charter Act of 1833 appointed the first Indian ICS officer.
Satyendranath Tagore was the first Indian to clear the ICS examination in 1864.
The Indian Civil Services Act, 1861 completely abolished restrictions on Indian entry.
accepted.x: The Indian Civil Services Act, 1861 permitted only limited Indian entry, and Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian to clear the ICS examination in 1864.
accepted.tq: Use the person-year association to reject statements that exaggerate the scope of the 1861 Act.
accepted.sec: Indians' share in administration and open competition → Act and committee  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Provincial dyarchy — Government of India Act, 1919
2. Provincial autonomy — Government of India Act, 1935
3. Central dyarchy — Government of India Act, 1935
4. Central dyarchy — Government of India Act, 1919
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
accepted.x: Provincial dyarchy was introduced by the Act of 1919, while provincial autonomy and proposed central dyarchy belonged to the Act of 1935. Pair 4 is incorrect.
accepted.tq: Separate the level of government before identifying the Act associated with dyarchy.
accepted.sec: Dyarchy - which Act introduced it, at which level, which Act ended it  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of reserved subjects under the provincial dyarchy introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919?
accepted.x: Police, finance and land revenue were reserved subjects administered by the Governor with the assistance of the Executive Council. Education, agriculture, public health and local self-government were transferred subjects.
accepted.tq: Separate the two columns of the dyarchy table before evaluating the set.
accepted.sec: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The central legislature under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms consisted of the:
o: Federal Assembly and Council of Provinces
House of Commons and House of Lords
Council of State and Legislative Assembly
Council of India and Executive Council
accepted.x: The central legislature consisted of the Council of State as the upper chamber and the Legislative Assembly as the lower chamber.
accepted.tq: Identify the two chambers by their exact official designations.
accepted.sec: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
The franchise under the central legislative arrangements associated with the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms was primarily restricted by qualifications relating to:
1. Property
2. Tax payment
3. Education
4. Universal adult suffrage
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
accepted.x: The franchise was limited and was based mainly on property, tax-payment and educational qualifications. Universal adult suffrage was not provided.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute modern-sounding alternative and identify the three restricted franchise bases.
accepted.sec: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The statutory commission contemplated under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms was appointed in 1927 under the chairmanship of:
accepted.x: The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927, two years before the expected review, and was chaired by Sir John Simon.
accepted.tq: Link the review commission with its year and chairman rather than with the reform’s authors.
accepted.sec: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the Simon Commission:
1. It was appointed in 1927, two years earlier than the scheduled review.
2. All its seven members were British.
3. It was chaired by Sir John Simon.
4. It was welcomed by Indian political organisations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: The Simon Commission was appointed in 1927, consisted of seven white members and was chaired by Sir John Simon. It was boycotted in India, so statement 4 is false.
accepted.tq: The final statement reverses the well-known response to the all-white commission.
accepted.sec: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The slogan associated with the boycott of the Simon Commission was:
accepted.x: The Simon Commission was boycotted in India under the slogan “Simon Go Back” because it had no Indian member.
accepted.tq: Use the commission’s composition to identify the slogan directly associated with its boycott.
accepted.sec: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following events is correctly associated with the anti-Simon Commission protest?
o: Lord Canning died after a protest at Lahore in 1927.
Satyendranath Tagore led the Lahore demonstration in 1854.
Sir John Simon was killed during the Lahore lathi-charge.
Lala Lajpat Rai died after the lathi-charge at Lahore in October 1928.
accepted.x: Lala Lajpat Rai died after sustaining injuries in the lathi-charge during the anti-Simon Commission protest at Lahore in October 1928.
accepted.tq: Keep the protest, place, year and person connected while rejecting swapped-person traps.
accepted.sec: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms - reserved and transferred subjects, central legislature, statutory commission  [GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the two levels of dyarchy contemplated by the Government of India Act, 1935?
o: Provincial dyarchy was introduced and central dyarchy operated fully from 1935.
Central dyarchy was introduced in 1919 and provincial dyarchy continued unchanged after 1935.
Provincial dyarchy was abolished, while proposed central dyarchy never took effect because the Federation did not come into existence.
Both provincial and central dyarchy were abolished by the Act of 1919.
accepted.x: The Act of 1935 replaced provincial dyarchy with provincial autonomy. Its proposed central dyarchy never came into operation because the Federation itself never came into existence.
accepted.tq: Compare the actual provincial change with the unimplemented federal provision.
accepted.sec: Dyarchy - which Act introduced it, at which level, which Act ended it  [APPSC, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: Which of the following statements best explains the significance of the Charter Act of 1833 in relation to central administration?
o: It created the office of the Secretary of State for India.
It introduced separate electorates for Muslims.
It vested legislative power for all British India in the Governor-General-in-Council.
accepted.x: The Charter Act of 1833 vested legislative power for all British India in the Governor-General-in-Council and marked a major step towards centralisation.
accepted.tq: Match the centralising legislative power with the Act that preceded the later separation under 1853.
accepted.sec: Separation of legislative and executive functions → Act  [other exams, GROUP-II]

accepted.s: The Ministry of Law and Justice traces its origin, as an organ of the Government of India, to the:
accepted.x: The Ministry of Law and Justice is traced to the Charter Act of 1833, which centralised legislative authority in the Governor-General-in-Council.
accepted.tq: Identify the institutional origin from the Act associated with centralised legislative authority.
accepted.sec: Separation of legislative and executive functions → Act  [other exams, GROUP-II]
